sourceSnapshot.basis: Authored corpus with merged overrides. File fingerprints identify the reviewed content independently of a branch name.

method.authoring: Agent-generated inventory, dependency extraction and proposed editorial triage from current merged content.
method.sourceDateRule: Only inheritedCheckedOn contains existing ledger dates. Null review fields mean no qualifying review is recorded here. generatedAt is an inventory timestamp, not source freshness.
method.scopeRule: Lesson scope, examples, assumptions and visual interpretation are copied from current merged content; they are not newly validated findings.
method.cadenceRule: Intervals and roles are proposals. Event-driven review and contributor judgment take priority; no owner or person has been assigned.

stable-principle.label: Stable principle
stable-principle.reason: The core mechanism is relatively stable. Review when scope, assumptions, diagrams or teaching examples change.

implementation-sensitive.label: Implementation sensitive
implementation-sensitive.reason: Implementations, software interfaces and engineering practice can change. Review at significant documentation or implementation revisions.

product-generation-sensitive.label: Product or generation sensitive
product-generation-sensitive.reason: Named architectures, process generations, interfaces and reference systems require configuration and version boundaries.

research-sensitive.label: Research interpretation sensitive
research-sensitive.reason: Research framing, model validity and replication status require explicit limitations and follow-up evidence.

status-sensitive.label: Announcement, deployment or forecast sensitive
status-sensitive.reason: Availability, readiness, allocation, forecast and announced specifications can change quickly; recheck on a status-changing event.

semiconductor-process-reviewer.label: Semiconductor process and device reviewer
semiconductor-process-reviewer.focus: Material and device assumptions, process order, metrology, units and generation limits.

computer-architecture-reviewer.label: Computer architecture and digital design reviewer
computer-architecture-reviewer.focus: Execution semantics, memory organization, circuit abstractions and named-generation boundaries.

packaging-systems-reviewer.label: Packaging, memory and machine integration reviewer
packaging-systems-reviewer.focus: Interfaces, assembly routes, compatibility, dimensions, yield and thermal assumptions.

infrastructure-engineering-reviewer.label: Power, cooling and infrastructure reviewer
infrastructure-engineering-reviewer.focus: IT/facility boundaries, usable capacity, thermal paths, network topology and commissioning evidence.

ml-systems-reviewer.label: ML systems and compiler reviewer
ml-systems-reviewer.focus: Software/version scope, tensor and memory semantics, workload conditions and performance denominators.

ml-methods-reviewer.label: ML methods and evaluation reviewer
ml-methods-reviewer.focus: Mathematical assumptions, training/inference distinctions, experimental scope and evaluation limits.

computation-realization-research-reviewe.label: Computation realization and research methods reviewer
computation-realization-research-reviewe.focus: Attribution, formal assumptions, claim boundaries, independent tests and separation of research framing from established results.

space-systems-reviewer.label: Space systems engineering reviewer
space-systems-reviewer.focus: Radiation, orbital energy/thermal/link budgets, measured demonstrations and lifecycle assumptions.

solid-state-device-reviewer.label: Solid-state physics and device reviewer
solid-state-device-reviewer.focus: Atomic/band models, carrier statistics, device regimes, dimensional consistency and conceptual visual mappings.

scienceModels.title: Every layer contributes to the thermal path

scope.role: Moves data between the server and the cluster network, often with direct-memory and protocol offloads.
scope.learningObjective: Separate fixed message startup time from payload transfer time on a network path.
scope.scale: Centimeter-scale adapter or module with external copper/optical links
scope.evidenceNotes: The lesson’s latency-plus-payload model uses decimal bytes and one direction. These are synthetic rates; the linked network references do not make this a promise about RDMA, GPU access, congestion or any deployed adapter.
scope.workedExample: Synthetic uncontended transfer: α = 5 μs and payload bandwidth = 25 GB/s. A 1 MB message needs 40 μs of serialization, giving about 45 μs total. A 1 kB message needs only 0.04 μs of serialization but still about 5.04 μs total, so startup dominates.

scienceModels.title: Small messages and large transfers have different bottlenecks
scienceModels.assumptions: A single uncontended path and approximately constant startup cost. Congestion, multiple hops, retransmission, protocol offloads, and overlap can change both terms. Convert bits per second to bytes per second before comparing them.

scope.learningObjective: Use Little’s law to relate average outstanding I/O, throughput and latency within one storage boundary.
scope.scale: Centimeter-scale module containing controller and NAND packages
scope.evidenceNotes: This is a steady-state queueing identity applied to the storage boundary, as explained by the lesson. I/O size, read/write mix, persistence requirements and latency definition must match; no product performance is inferred.
scope.workedExample: Synthetic stable workload: 100,000 IOPS at 200 μs average latency implies 100,000 × 0.0002 = 20 average outstanding operations. Doubling submitted queue depth does not imply double IOPS, because latency and the limiting resource may also change.

scienceModels.title: High IOPS requires enough outstanding work
scienceModels.assumptions: Little’s law applied to a stable workload with a consistent measurement boundary. Latency generally changes with load, so the relation does not promise constant latency at arbitrary queue depth; read size, write mix, and durability requirements matter.

scope.role: Converts a distribution voltage into tightly controlled low-voltage rails for processors and memory.
scope.learningObjective: Estimate the duty cycle and inductor ripple of an ideal buck converter while keeping the power-stage assumptions explicit.
scope.scale: Centimeter-scale circuit around the processor; millimeter power components
scope.evidenceNotes: The relation is the lesson’s ideal continuous-conduction model. Switch losses, control dynamics, phase cancellation, saturation and discontinuous conduction are excluded; the cited power-conversion sources supply the physical context.
scope.workedExample: Synthetic buck stage: 12 V input and 1 V output imply D = 1/12. With L = 1 μH and switching frequency 1 MHz, ΔI ≈ (12 − 1) × (1/12)/(1 μH × 1 MHz) ≈ 0.917 A peak-to-peak. These values describe one hypothetical stage, not a GPU regulator.

scienceModels.title: Inductor volt-seconds set the ideal buck ratio
scienceModels.assumptions: Ideal continuous-conduction buck stage with fixed input/output voltage and negligible switch losses. Multiphase cancellation, nonlinear inductors, dead time, control dynamics, and discontinuous conduction require further analysis; no GPU power-stage values are assumed.

scope.visualInterpretation: Conversion stages step from facility distribution to low-voltage chip supplies. Geometry exposes stages, not an installation wiring plan.

The bound is an I/O boundary, not a complete recovery policy.

The local E5 journal/receipt replay is executable. It is separate from the operating hall’s retained computational-work model and from actual distributed training checkpoint formats.

Mode: executable full checkpoint. Exact equality is tested within one numerical implementation and operation order. scope.workedExample:
A 2 TB checkpoint at 20 GB/s has a lower-bound transfer time of 100 seconds before metadata, contention and consistency work.

The incident journal can end at a valid approved reservation intent while its environment already stores reservation-1. Restoring only that journal does not return the two consumed FILTER-A units. Recovery checks the one pending service against the environment receipt and returns the original outcome. In contrast, restoring a training checkpoint can repeat arithmetic from saved parameters but cannot by itself undo inventory in a separate service.

An automated fixture trains 17 updates, exports the complete checkpoint, restores it and performs 23 more. Its weights, moments, RNG, draw counter and history exactly match 40 uninterrupted updates in the same deterministic binary64 implementation. With two sampled examples per update, the final draw count is 80. Restoring only weights while resetting moments produces a different next trajectory.

scope.role: Turn text into a sequence of discrete IDs.
scope.learningObjective: Compare token counts for identical text and explain how they affect a sequence budget.

scope.evidenceNotes:
Counts are invented to illustrate the lesson’s identity, not outputs of a named tokenizer. Real comparisons require the identical text, tokenizer version and control-token rules; languages and code do not share a universal bytes/token ratio.

Mode: worked example. Toy word boundaries and deterministic lexical tie rule; no byte fallback or production BPE trainer is executed by the core. Numerical examples are authored calculations, except explicitly identified automated core fixtures. Primary sources support the scoped mechanism; no human specialist review or learner outcome is implied.

The implemented whole-field UTF-8 byte variant has no word pre-tokenizer and can merge across spaces within a field. Smaller token count is not by itself evidence of better learning. BPE IDs never enter the fixed nine-token lifecycle decoder.
scope.workedExample:
Synthetic text has 24 UTF-8 bytes. Tokenizer A returns 6 IDs and tokenizer B returns 8, giving 4 and 3 bytes/token respectively. At fixed per-token cached state, B needs 8/6 ≈ 1.33× as much cache for this text; the ratio is about encoding, not understanding.

Use training words “aa” twice and “ab” once, represented as character sequences with no cross-word pairs. Pair (a,a) has count 2 and (a,b) count 1, so the first merge forms aa. Encoding held-out “aab” yields [aa,b] under this toy merge list. Letting held-out “ab” occurrences change the winning pair would change both input IDs and evaluation token denominators.

In the field abab, the pair ab occurs twice. One merge maps its two bytes to a new symbol, and encoding becomes two copies of that symbol. In aaa, the pair aa has two overlapping counts but only one non-overlapping replacement. These counts describe different stages of the algorithm.

scienceModels.title: Sequence length is an engineering variable
scienceModels.assumptions: Compare identical text, a specified tokenizer version, and the same treatment of control tokens. There is no universal bytes-per-token constant, especially across languages and code.

scope.workedExample:
For sequence length T, the unstructured score matrix has T² entries per head; memory-aware kernels change movement without changing the mathematical dependency.

Synthetic vector [1, 3] has mean 2 and population variance 1. With unit scale, zero shift and ε = 0.00001, LayerNorm gives approximately [−0.999995, 0.999995]. Separately, adding an update [0.5, −0.5] to the original vector gives [1.5, 2.5]; the two operations do different work.

scope.workedExample:
Synthetic logits [0, ln 2, ln 3] exponentiate to [1, 2, 3], so softmax gives [1/6, 1/3, 1/2]. Greedy decoding chooses the third candidate; sampling can choose any of the three. A two-token sequence with conditional probabilities 1/2 then 1/4 has probability 1/8.

A sample different from the greedy class is not evidence that the probabilities or gradient were incorrectly computed.

scope.workedExample:
Synthetic layer has eight experts with 1 million parameters each, plus 2 million shared parameters, and selects two experts per token. Stored parameters total 10 million; the simplified selected count is 4 million. At two bytes per stored parameter, weights occupy 20 MB before metadata.

Six tokens dispatch to three experts with counts [3,2,1], so f=[1/2,1/3,1/6]. Mean router probabilities are P=[1/2,1/3,1/6]. With alpha=0.01 and N=3, auxiliary loss is 0.01×3×(1/4+1/9+1/36)=0.011667. These are computed relationships in twelve authored documents across seven known families. No language-model quality, memorization rate or representative real-corpus coverage is measured.
scope.workedExample:
Synthetic source losses are 2 and 4 under the same loss definition. Sampling weights 0.75 and 0.25 give mixture loss 2.5; changing to 0.5 and 0.5 gives 3. The calculation changes source influence even when total example count is unchanged.

If a training-only normalizer has mean 60 and standard deviation 10, input 70 maps to 1. Recomputing a mean of 70 using a later population maps the same input to 0. Comparing model predictions before and after that change as if only the weights mattered hides a preprocessing change. The new artifact lesson gives a logistic example where the resulting threshold decision reverses.

The executable corpus has 12 training, 8 development and 4 final examples per domain. Across copy and swap this is 24/16/8 example records, but only 12/8/4 distinct prompt families because each domain assigns its own answer to the same family. Treating all 48 records as independent prompt families would double-count the evidence.

At split seed17 in the original maintenance fixture, splitting individual documents places fan7-original in training and its exact mirror in evaluation. Whole-family assignment removes that flagged cross-split overlap. At default seed7, exact-copy exclusion removes three training records while preserving their original texts and retained-document pointers.

scope.scale: Logical structure · mapped onto physical hardware
scope.evidenceNotes:
This follows the ordinary Adam equations in the linked paper. The gradient is supplied rather than derived here; clipping, weight decay, loss scaling and sharded optimizer state are excluded. Computing a gradient and applying an update remain separate steps.

The threshold arithmetic is authored. The existing sensor experience executes actual logistic updates, while these three probabilities are a separate worked decision example.

Mode: executable derived-gradient optimizer. No weight decay or AMSGrad; elementwise squares/division. First-step worked values use an unclipped scalar gradient of 0.5. Numerical examples are authored calculations, except explicitly identified automated core fixtures. Primary sources support the scoped mechanism; no human specialist review or learner outcome is implied.
scope.workedExample:
Synthetic first Adam step: θ = 1, gradient g = 2, zero initial moments, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999 and learning rate 0.01 give m₁ = 0.2 and v₁ = 0.004. Bias correction gives m̂₁ = 2 and v̂₁ = 4; with ε = 10⁻⁸, θ becomes approximately 0.99.

For fixed predicted probabilities [0.2,0.6,0.8], a threshold of 0.5 gives decisions [0,1,1], while threshold 0.7 gives [0,0,1]. The weights and all three probabilities are unchanged. With labels [0,0,1], the second threshold removes one false positive on these three cases. This does not prove that 0.7 is better on future data; selecting it using the held-out test would also compromise that test’s independence.

For a scalar gradient g=0.5, weight 2 and learning rate 0.1, SGD gives 1.95. For the first Adam step with zero moments, beta1=0.9 and beta2=0.999, m=0.05 and v=0.00025; bias-corrected values are 0.5 and 0.25. With epsilon=1e-8 the Adam result is approximately 1.900000002. It differs from SGD because Adam normalizes by the second-moment scale.

scienceModels.title: Adam adapts updates using gradient moments
scienceModels.assumptions: Products, squares, and divisions are coordinate-wise. With zero initialization, m̂ₜ=mₜ/(1−β₁ᵗ) and v̂ₜ=vₜ/(1−β₂ᵗ). This is ordinary Adam; decoupled weight decay, clipping, loss scaling, and distributed sharding require additional rules.

The incident policy is explicitly authored. The extension distinguishes behavioral system changes from actual weight adaptation and makes no claim of new post-training execution.

Mode: executable SFT DPO and bandit. Core conventions: answer plus EOS SFT, response-pair DPO, one-action bandit rollouts. These are not a claim that every post-training implementation uses the same denominators. Numerical examples are authored calculations, except explicitly identified automated core fixtures. scope.workedExample:
Synthetic comparison with β = 0.5: response policy A has expected reward 2 and KL divergence 0.4 nats, giving objective 1.8. Policy B has reward 1.9 and KL 0.1 nats, giving 1.85. The penalized objective favors B even though its raw reward is lower.

The same fictional malformed quantity is rejected in both incident modes. The fixed workflow stops; the authored branching policy repairs the string into an integer and continues. This behavior difference comes entirely from application control code, with no trained model or parameter update. It is useful engineering progress, but it is not evidence of post-training a language model.

For a batch of two one-turn demonstrations with answer plus EOS, SFT averages four target losses. Two DPO comparisons instead average two pair losses. The core reward branch samples four answers for each of two prompts and averages eight rollout terms. Their numerical loss values have different denominators and meanings; a lower DPO number is not directly better than a higher SFT number.

scope.role: Connect model inference to actions and evidence.
scope.learningObjective: Track which state changes in a tool-assisted inference loop and account for its sequential latency.
scope.scale: Logical structure · mapped onto physical hardware
scope.evidenceNotes:
The model–action–observation pattern follows the linked Toolformer/ReAct context. Times are synthetic; parallel tools, failure, retries and context management alter timing. The runtime validates permissions and results rather than treating a proposal as completed work.

The executable extension is a fictional local environment with two authored policies. It adds no claim of real LLM agency, MCP conformance or production durability. Model parameters, invocation context and the workflow journal remain separate objects.

Mode: worked example. Authored finite inventory contract, not an actual external order. Model generation, validator execution and learning updates have separate state boundaries. Numerical examples are authored calculations, except explicitly identified automated core fixtures. Primary sources support the scoped mechanism; no human specialist review or learner outcome is implied.
scope.workedExample:
Synthetic loop: first model call takes 0.8 s, a permitted tool takes 0.3 s, and the follow-up model call takes 0.7 s. With sequential execution, elapsed time is 1.8 s before overhead. Tool output changes the next call’s context; it does not by itself update the model’s learned weights.

In the commit-timeout case, reserving two FILTER-A units leaves two of the original four units before the caller has any successful response. The fixed workflow retries the same keyed action; the authored policy looks up the receipt. Both can finish with one reservation and one work order. Neither can infer that the timeout meant no effect occurred.

In an authored inventory environment, stock starts at 3. A proposed reserve(2) passes a bound of available stock and commits stock=1. Retrying the same committed action with the same idempotency key returns its prior receipt rather than subtracting again. A fresh reserve(2) fails because only one remains. Saying “reserved” after that rejection is an answer failure even if its JSON syntax is valid.

scienceModels.assumptions: This is a schematic sequential loop, not a hidden implementation. Tools may fail, be asynchronous, or change external state; the runtime enforces permissions and can decline actions. Context management may summarize rather than retain all history.

scope.role: Measure breadth, reliability, and practical competence.
scope.learningObjective: Use a proportion with uncertainty rather than a single pass rate.
scope.scale: Logical structure · mapped onto physical hardware
scope.evidenceNotes:
Benchmark selection, contamination, rubric and dependence dominate many real evaluations.

The examples use fictional environments and deterministic authored policies. They do not reproduce τ-bench cases or establish a real agent’s reliability or benchmark score.

Mode: executable final report; worked uncertainty. Independent Bernoulli sampling model for the illustrative interval; the authored four-case split is not demonstrated to be a representative population sample. Interval does not cure dataset selection bias. Numerical examples are authored calculations, except explicitly identified automated core fixtures. Primary sources support the scoped mechanism; no human specialist review or learner outcome is implied.
scope.workedExample:
If k=90 of n=100 items pass, p̂=0.9; the standard-error approximation is about 0.03 under a simple independent-sample model.

In the wrong-entity incident, the authored policy completes one FAN-9 work order supported by the FAN-9 manual. Source support is 1/1, yet the original FAN-7 task is wrong. In the canceled-after-commit case the reservation exists but the required work order does not, so task success is false even though an external write succeeded. These outcomes expose errors that counting successful calls would miss.

A result of 4/4 on the tiny final copy split is 100% observed accuracy, not proof of perfect population accuracy. A Wilson 95% interval with z=1.96 has lower bound about 0.510 and upper bound 1.000. The finite test supports only its declared toy task and split. Updating weights after the report changes model identity; the earlier 4/4 must remain attributed to the earlier checkpoint.

scienceModels.title: Benchmark success has sampling uncertainty
scienceModels.assumptions: Binary outcomes, independent trials, fixed conditions, and a representative sample are required. The plug-in approximation is poor near zero or one or with small n; use suitable binomial intervals. Correlated tasks, benchmark selection, contamination, and judge error add other uncertainties.

scope.workedExample:
Synthetic graph: Y = maximum(XW + b, 0) contains a dot, broadcasted bias add and activation. With X of shape 4×8 and two-byte elements, X has 64 logical bytes before padding or replication.

For X=[[1,2]] and W=[[3],[4]], XW is [[11]]. Adding bias −12 and applying ReLU gives [[0]]. Applying ReLU before adding the bias instead gives [[−1]], so moving operations because their intermediate shapes match changes the function. A legal fusion can eliminate materialized intermediates only while preserving the specified order and result.

scope.workedExample:
Synthetic 4×8 row-major tensor has strides (8,1). Swapping logical axes can produce an 8×4 view with strides (1,8), avoiding a copy until a consumer demands contiguous rows.

hbf-latency-prefetch.title: HBF latency, transfer granularity and prefetch

scope.role: Explain why matching read bandwidth does not guarantee matching request latency or useful-byte efficiency.
scope.learningObjective: Explain why matching read bandwidth does not guarantee matching request latency or useful-byte efficiency.
scope.scale: Request granularity, queues and staging buffers; abstract dataflow
scope.evidenceNotes: The Sandisk fact sheet’s comparison concerns internal testing/simulation of reading 8-bit pretrained Llama 3.1 405B weights, one kernel at a time on an xPU performance model. It does not establish arbitrary random reads, training writes or end-to-end serving parity. KIOXIA supports general NAND access distinctions, not HBF timing numbers.
scope.workedExample: Synthetic access: 1 TB/s with 20 µs completion latency requires at least 20 MB outstanding in the simple concurrency model. A 16 KiB fetch with only 1 KiB consumed has 6.25% useful-byte efficiency. Neither latency nor granularity is an HBF product specification.

scienceModels.title: Useful-byte efficiency
scienceModels.assumptions: 0 < u ≤ g, no later use of the remaining bytes; this is traffic efficiency, not a measured HBF result.

scienceModels.title: Concurrency to cover latency
scienceModels.assumptions: Steady independent requests, adequate resources, no contention or dependency stalls; necessary capacity is not sufficient throughput proof.

sharded-matmul-ownership.title: Sharded matrix multiplication and result ownership

scope.role: Derive the communication operation from the partitioned matrix axis and the next consumer’s required result layout.
scope.learningObjective: Reconstruct the same 2×2 product from inner-dimension shards, choose a collective from output ownership, and reconcile the two-rank payload ledger.

scope.workedExample: Use A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[5,6],[7,8]]. Rank 0 owns k=0 and forms C₀ = [[5,6],[15,18]]; rank 1 owns k=1 and forms C₁ = [[14,16],[28,32]]. Reduce-scatter with row ownership sends C₀ row 1 [15,18] from rank 0 to rank 1, and C₁ row 0 [14,16] in the opposite direction. Rank 0 adds [5,6]+[14,16]=[19,22]; rank 1 adds [15,18]+[28,32]=[43,50]. Each sends 8 payload bytes if elements are float32. If both consumers need all of C, all-gather exchanges these completed rows for another 8 bytes sent per rank. Both then hold [[19,22],[43,50]]. Total sent payload is 16 bytes per rank, 32 across the two senders; counting the matching receives again would double-count this network boundary. Concatenating the two original 2×2 partial matrices would create four rows and would leave their sums unfinished.

distributed-gradient-weighting.title: Uneven batches and the global gradient

scope.role: Preserve the intended training objective when ranks contribute different numbers of valid examples or tokens.
scope.learningObjective: Derive and test a globally normalized gradient from unequal local batch means, then distinguish objective equivalence from replica synchronization.
scope.scale: Logical values and distributed ownership; no physical scale or vendor timing
scope.evidenceNotes: The PyTorch source is pinned to v2.8.0 and supports the default averaging convention, not a claim about every backend or custom hook. The squared-error data, gradient weighting derivation and SGD step are authored examples. Join semantics after input exhaustion are outside this fixed-participant update.
scope.workedExample: Take ℓ(w;y)=½(w−y)² at w=10. Rank 0 has targets [9,9], producing gradients [1,1], count 2 and mean 1. Rank 1 has [7,7,7,7,7,7], producing six gradients of 3, count 6 and mean 3. The unpartitioned objective has gradient (2×1+6×3)/8=2.5. Averaging rank means gives (1+3)/2=2 instead. With learning rate 0.1, correct SGD gives wnew=9.75; the unweighted rank mean gives 9.8. For a reducer that divides by P=2, scale the local means by 2×2/8=0.5 and 2×6/8=1.5. It then averages 0.5 and 4.5 to obtain 2.5. If the ranks each held four valid items, equal weighting would be appropriate. Token-level training needs the valid target-token count when that is the declared loss denominator; sequence counts need not be proportional.

speculative-decoding-verification.title: Speculative decoding: proposals and verified output

scope.role: Account for target-distributed output tokens while separating draft work, verification and actual elapsed time.
scope.learningObjective: Recover the target distribution by exact probability accounting, then calculate output-per-round and a conditional throughput without treating proposals or assumptions as measured useful output.
scope.scale: Logical values and distributed ownership; no physical scale or vendor timing
scope.evidenceNotes: The cited ICML paper establishes the strict correction algorithm and the explicitly iid output-count formula. The toy probabilities, output-count distribution and all millisecond values are authored. No private model, serving implementation, benchmark speedup or quality improvement is asserted.
scope.workedExample: For symbols A/B/C, choose target p=[0.6,0.3,0.1] and draft q=[0.2,0.3,0.5]. Conditional acceptance is [1,1,0.2], so accepted probability mass is [0.2,0.3,0.1] and total α=0.6. The rejected mass is 0.4; normalized positive residual p−q is [1,0,0], so every correction in this toy case is A. The final output distribution is [0.2,0.3,0.1]+0.4×[1,0,0]=[0.6,0.3,0.1], exactly the target distribution. If γ=2 and acceptance events are independently 0.6 at both positions, output counts 1,2,3 have probabilities 0.4,0.24,0.36. Thus E[K]=1.96 tokens. Separately assume the two draft steps together take 2 ms, target verification 6 ms and overhead 1 ms: 1.96/0.009≈217.8 output tokens/s. A 6 ms single-token baseline would be 166.7 tokens/s under those assumptions. At 12 ms verification, the speculative scenario instead gives 130.7 tokens/s. Neither timing is measured or taken from the paper; acceptance alone does not establish acceleration.

scope.learningObjective: Compute loaded delay and conservative DC noise margins, recognize the ideal model’s vertical transition, and distinguish load-induced timing failure from electrical asymmetry.
scope.scale: Declared 2 μm channel, nanometre oxide inputs and one lumped circuit; schematic geometry
scope.evidenceNotes: The physical equations and conventions are primary-source informed. The parameter values, corners, constraints and results are authored teaching choices; no commercial process or human specialist review is represented.
scope.workedExample: With default INV-01, VIL=0.5364598 V, VIH=0.6635402 V, VOL=0.0635402 V and VOH=1.1364598 V. Both noise margins are 0.4729196 V; the 50% step delay is 0.6997759 ns in each direction. Four following loads increase total capacitance to 230.99584 fF and delay to 2.4773623 ns, while all four static voltages and noise margins remain unchanged. The 1 ns timing gate fails. Reducing nMOS mobility to 0.5× and adding 120 mV to its threshold instead produces a 1.8745095 ns falling delay and 0.3967162 V high noise margin, failing the chosen 0.4 V noise requirement as well.

scienceModels.title: Piecewise long-channel current magnitude
scienceModels.assumptions: Long-channel, strong-inversion, constant mobility, no channel-length modulation, leakage, body-bias changes or short-channel effects. Ideal cutoff is not real subthreshold behavior.

scienceModels.title: One output load connects to the following gates
scienceModels.assumptions: Constant full oxide-area approximation, not voltage-dependent gate capacitance. The extra load is supplied, not an extracted wire/junction model; intrinsic and overlap parasitics are omitted.

scienceModels.title: Loaded delay from the current integral
scienceModels.assumptions: Instantaneous rail-to-rail input step, one conducting pull device, constant load and ideal initial rail. These are mathematical model times, not measured silicon delays. The output approaches its final rail asymptotically.

scienceModels.title: Use the actual unity-gain output levels
scienceModels.assumptions: Static cascade convention for identical gates in the declared model; no noise spectrum, transient susceptibility, error rate or statistical distribution is predicted.

scope.visualInterpretation: A schematic complementary device pair shares an input and drives a load. The enlarged gate dielectric and capacitive load expose distinct physical roles. Geometry is conceptual; the electrical experience computes the named long-channel specimen, transfer curve and timed transition.
